title: Joy and ease
hook: steps five and six: breathing with gladness, breathing with ease

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole body: steps three and four, feeling it all and letting it calm. Your line was the body settles. Did your shoulders drop today? Day one hundred and ten.

Meditation has a reputation for being a bit like flossing. Good for you, mildly unpleasant, something to get through. So it's a surprise when the Buddhist breathing discourse, at step five, says: breathe with joy. And at step six: breathe with ease. Not grim endurance. Gladness. And there's a story behind that, one you already know from camp two. A young man, starving himself in the forest, suddenly remembers a happy afternoon from long ago, and asks himself a question that changes everything.
screen: `MEDITATION AS FLOSSING?` → `BREATHE WITH JOY.` → `A QUESTION THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Remember the rose-apple tree. In a discourse called the Mahasaccaka Sutta, after he has pushed his body through harsh practice to the edge of death, the Buddha-to-be recalls a day long before, sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree while his father was busy, and slipping into a quiet, happy stillness. And he asks himself: why am I afraid of that pleasure? It has nothing to do with craving or harm. That question turned him toward the middle way. Steps five and six carry the same insight. The person trains: experiencing joy, I will breathe in and out. Experiencing ease, I will breathe in and out. Today's word is piti, joy or rapture: the bright, lifting, sometimes tingling gladness that can arise when the mind settles. Its partner is sukha, a softer happiness, ease, contentment. The old manual, the Visuddhimagga, tells them apart with a picture. A traveler lost in the desert, exhausted, sees a pool of water up ahead: that's piti, the thrill. Then he reaches it, drinks, and bathes: that's sukha, the deep ease. Both are welcome. Both are part of the path. Now, you don't manufacture these feelings. When the body settles, as it did in steps three and four, pleasure tends to show up on its own: warmth, lightness, a quiet smile. The practice is simply to let it in, instead of brushing it off as a distraction. That can be the hard part, if you've learned to trust only effort and discomfort. The discourse trains the other way. You're allowed to enjoy it.
screen: `WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT PLEASURE?` · `PITI: JOY. SUKHA: EASE.` · `THE POOL SEEN, THE POOL REACHED.` · `LET IT IN.` · then, large: `YOU'RE ALLOWED TO ENJOY IT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the body settle, the way you did yesterday. Now look for anything pleasant, however small: the warmth of your hands, the softness of the out-breath, the quiet in the room, the relief of sitting down. Don't create anything. Just find what's already there. When you notice something pleasant, let it be felt, fully, for a breath or two. If nothing seems pleasant, notice what's neutral and easy; that counts too. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Piti. Joy, gladness, the bright lift that can come when the mind settles. Step five of the breath.
Your line: you're allowed to enjoy it. Today, when something is pleasant, a meal, the sun, a laugh, stay with it for one extra breath. Day one hundred and ten.

howItsDone: Following these steps, Buddhist meditation teachers encourage students to notice and allow the joy (piti) and ease (sukha) that arise as the mind settles, rather than treating practice as grim effort.

match.prompt: what's inside the steps — tap the pairs.

myth: Buddhist meditation is meant to feel grim
steps five and six are breathing with joy and breathing with ease.
the rose-apple memory led the Buddha to ask why he feared that pleasure
in the Mahasaccaka Sutta, that question turned him toward the middle way.
piti and sukha are exactly the same
piti is the thrill of seeing the pool; sukha is the ease of drinking from it.

fork.setup: you're meditating, and a warm, happy feeling rises. what do the steps suggest?
options: push it away as a distraction.
let it be felt, and breathe with it.
chase it and try to make it bigger.
fork.reveal: steps five and six train you to breathe experiencing joy and ease: let it in without chasing it.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation should feel nice.
what it means: joy and ease that come when the mind settles are part of the path, to be allowed, not chased.
what a scholar hears: piti and sukha are two factors of the first jhana; the desert-traveler simile distinguishing them is in Visuddhimagga IV.

Editor review (days 95–112): MN 36 does not say 'six years' or 'as a boy' (those come from later tradition and the commentary), so the teach now follows the sutta: harsh practice to the edge of death, then the memory of the rose-apple shade while his father was busy. Hook no longer claims what 'a lot of people' expect; cut 'for many people that's the hard part'.
